utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. While the witness is being brought in, I'd mention that on Friday just before we finished it was moved by the Defence for the admission of an overview of recorded criminal offences. The Chamber has come to the view that it should receive only those passages that dealt with offences that the witness was able to speak about. They were each in turn put to the witness in the course of the hearing. We will receive each of those as an exhibit. We will not receive any other part of the overview on the basis of the present evidence. Because this is in total but a very small part of the whole document, the Chamber would direct that the Defence prepare a document which includes only those summaries that were put to the witness. Once it's checked with the Prosecution, the Chamber will then treat that as the exhibit. That ought to be done in the course of this week I would imagine. There are two other procedural motions. From the 22nd of February, the Prosecution sought leave to upload a missing page of Exhibit P1029. It was the Blue Book of the OSCE. The Chamber would authorise that missing page to be uploaded and form part of the present exhibit. On the same day, the Prosecution indicated that it had received an official translation of the document marked for identification as P1532. The Chamber will grant leave for that to be uploaded into e-court. When that is done, the document presently marked MFI P1532 should become an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will you please read aloud the affirmation shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Please sit down. Mr. Popovic has some questions for you. Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, before I start asking questions of you, I will ask you that after you hear the question I asked, wait for a moment before you start answering because we both speak the same language. We will thus enable the interpreters to do their work properly, and I will also ask you to speak slowly so that they may be able to correctly interpret what you are going to say. Please start by stating your full name.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Branko Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When were you born and where?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 22nd of August, 1968 at Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, were you a member of the Ministry of the Interior, or are you still staff of that ministry?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was a member of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia since 1988, and I still am.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain briefly your duties in the Ministry of the Interior during your career so far.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: After graduating from the secondary school of the Ministry of the Interior at Vucitrn, I worked as a police officer at the Prizren police station. After that, in 1989 I was sent to Urosevac where I was also a police officer at the police station. For a while I was a chief of sector at the Urosevac police station. For a brief period I was the assistant shift commander, and after that the shift commander of the duty service of the SUP of Urosevac. From 1993 till 1996 I was inspector at the criminal police combatting drug addiction and drug smuggling. And from 1996 through 1998 I worked as the assistant commander of the police station of Urosevac. Since the 1st of June, 1998, and until the end of 1999 I was commander of the Stimlje police station. After the Kosovo police secretariats were relocated to the Republic of Serbia, I worked in the territory of the Smederevo police administration. In 2001 I was deputy company commander of the Belgrade detachment of the gendarmerie in Belgrade, and from 2002 to 2006 I worked as inspector for violent crime and sexual offences at the Smederevo police administration. From 2006, so -- sorry, yes -- well, from 2006 till now I have worked as chief of the department for foreigner -- for foreigners for the combatting of human smuggling and smuggling in general in Smederevo, which work I still do today.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Mladenovic, during my examination I will focus mostly on 1998 and 1999. You have already said what you said at that time. So speaking about the Stimlje police station, can you tell us which territory was covered by your police station, that is, from the 1st of June, 1998, when you were appointed commander of the Stimlje police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: At that time the Stimlje police station covered the territory of the Stimlje municipality, including the surrounding villages, Muzicane, Vojnovci, Davidovci, Rasince, Gornje and Donje Godance, then the village of Petrovic, Petrastica, Duga, Karacica, and Zborce, the village of Crnoljevo, Rance, Racak, Malo Poljce, and Petrovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What were your powers when you were commander of the Stimlje police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: As commander of the Stimlje police station, I had the competences as laid out by the Law on Internal Affairs, namely to protect the lives and security of persons and their property, the prevention and clearing up of criminal offences, identifying and finding the perpetrators of criminal offences. Activities had to do with traffic control, the protection of public law and order, securing certain persons and facilities, public rallies and gatherings, as well as certain administrative business with regard to citizenship, personal IDs, travel documents, driving licences, and the registration of motor vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was your immediate superior in 1998 and 1999? Speaking of these two years, I'm always referring to the period starting with the day when you were appointed commander of the police station in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 and 1999 my immediate superior was the chief of the department of the police, Mr. Radomir Mitic, and the chief of the SUP of Urosevac, Bogoljub Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Were these persons the ones from whom you received commands and orders and instructions while you were commander of the police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Let me try and clarify this. Every -- all the tasks that I have listed are part of my legal obligation. So each police officer, including myself as a commander, was duty-bound to adhere by the law and act in accordance with the rules, the rule book about the carrying out of our jobs and tasks. Certain instructions and orders certainly came in from my immediate superior, the chief of the department of the police, Radomir Mitic, and the chief of the SUP, Bogoljub Janicevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic. Speaking about the Stimlje police station and the years 1998 and 1999, can you try to explain to us what the security situation in the territory covered by your police station was in 1998 and immediately before the NATO forces started bombing?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In 1998 the political situation that previously was very bad in the territory covered by the Stimlje police station, that is, the municipality of Stimlje, was very bad and problematic mostly because in early 1998 there was a huge escalation of terrorism, certain terrorist groups that sprung up in that period received support in the surrounding villages which were in a hilly area covered with forests which made police control difficult. And speaking about Petrastica, Zborce, Duga and Karacica. Then the village of Crnoljevo, Rance, Racak, Malo Poljce, and Petrovo. In those villages, the Albanian terrorists in 1998 established their staffs, and later they forced the civilian population to take up arms, dig trenches and fortifications, that they would use to attack the police and the state bodies of the Republic of Serbia. Due to this very bad situation the police station couldn't protect the civilian population and help them because every -- our attempt to go to those villages resulted in an attack on my patrols by the Albanian terrorists. In that period a certain number of police officers was killed, and in early, or rather, in June 1998 the Pristina-Prizren highway through Crnoljevo, the Crnoljevo canyon, was completely blocked. That is, the Albanian terrorists gained control over that road. And they kidnapped several dozen citizens of Serb ethnicity and some individuals of other ethnicity who did not support their activity and their fight.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. I do apologise, but if I can, I would like to finish. I keep following this.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Please go on.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This situation made it necessary to do the following. These villages where the terrorists had organised themselves, and those are the villages I mentioned a few moments ago, Albanian civilians started moving out of these villages and sought refuge in Stimlje, Urosevac, Lipljan, Pristina. They were under the control of the police. After that, a police action followed by the police staff for combatting terrorism from Pristina. So these strongholds were crushed and up until the 12th of June, 1999, while we kept this area under control, the civilian population never actually returned to these villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic. I'm sure we'll discuss this in greater detail during your testimony today. I would be interested in the following. Could you please explain to us the role of communication that you mentioned -- actually, the road between Pristina and Prizren. What was the importance of that road in general. And did that road go through the town of Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This road was very important. It linked the capital of Kosovo, Pristina, with Metohija, Prizren-Pec-Djakovica, and it went through Stimlje, Crnoljevo, that Crnoljevo gorge through Dulje to Suva Reka and Prizren. It was important because that was the only road there. There was an alternative road, but that was much longer via Urosevac, Brezovica, Prevalce, all the way to Prizren. This road was very important. It is a road which is like an artery for the life of the civilian population of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic. I'm just going to ask you, for the purpose of the transcript, when you spoke about this situation over the past few minutes, did you speak about the security situation in the territory of the police station of Stimlje?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I spoke of how difficult the situation was in the territory of the police station of Stimlje because Stimlje as a municipality borders with Drenica, where the major stronghold of the Albanian terrorists was. The forests around these villages were convenient for the Albanian terrorists. They hid in those forests and they used the civilian population as a human shield. They exercised violence against them. The state organs and the police station of Stimlje were called upon to protect the civilian population.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Page 5, line 23, says that you'd spoke about the political situation, but it was actually the security situation. Mr. Mladenovic, I would like to show you some documents, and I would like to hear your comments. With the permission of the Court yet again we are going to use a binder that we prepared for this witness. Every time when I call up a certain document on the screen, I'm going to tell you what number that is in your binder.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Now I would like us to look at P357.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: That's number 1 in your binder, Mr. Mladenovic. These are rules about the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior, the 31st of December, 1987 is the date. I would be interested in Article 4, paragraph 31. It's page 8 in the B/C/S version, and I think it is something similar in English or perhaps it's page 6 in English. Could we just wait for a moment to see the document on our screens. It's not the right page in English. I need Article 4.31. It's two pages before the page that we see now in English. And in B/C/S, yes, it's the right page. Yes. While we're waiting for that page to appear -- yes, yes, this is the right page in English as well. Mr. Mladenovic, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am. And it speaks of the internal organisation of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Serbia from the period of 1987 in Article 4 it says --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Article 4, please let us look at 31.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 31. It says that Urosevac was established as a secretariat for the area of the municipality of Urosevac, Kacanik, Stimlje, and Strpce. In 31 it is the SUP Urosevac and then there is a department in Kacanik.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says in Urosevac a department of the interior of the municipality of Kacanik and police stations in the municipalities of Stimlje and Strpce.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that is that Article 4. It actually defines the internal organisation of the secretariat in Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: These rules also define the work and responsibilities of the police station of Stimlje, or rather, police stations in general, thereby Stimlje as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Since we're discussing this, could you please look at Article 48. It should be page 36 in the English or try 39.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Article 48 defines the role of the police stations, which is the following. Police stations shall ensure the safety of citizens and their property on the territory of the municipality for which they have been established and perform any other internal affairs related tasks on that territory within their sphere of activity. They shall directly perform tasks in the prevention and detection of crimes, the discovery and apprehension of the perpetrators of crimes and their transfer into the custody of the competent organs --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, we don't need to read the entire paragraph because we have it here before us in writing. Could we just hear your brief comment. Were these actually the responsibilities that you had and the work that you carried out at the Stimlje police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was the work and duties conducted by the police station in Stimlje, the so-called regular work and duties of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at the last sentence in this article that says: "Police stations may include departments as well ..." Did you have police departments within your police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: We did not, but in the period of 1998 after the agreement reached between Milosevic and Holbrooke a temporary branch police station was established in the village of Crnoljevo in order to secure the road between Pristina and Stimlje and then moving on to Crnoljevo, Suva Reka, and Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic. Tell me, the work and duties you conducted at your police station, did they fall under the regular police work and duties of the public security of the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, only that. The police station in Stimlje carried out only that work for which it was organised and that they were supposed to carry out on the basis of these rules and the law. There was no other work that was carried out by the policemen of the police station in Stimlje. This was regular police work, stemming from these laws and regulations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In order to be more specific within your answer, the police station in Stimlje, or rather, the members of that police station, were you ever involved in carrying out special security-related police work in the territory of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: No. It was the staff and the special police units that were in charge of that. We were not involved in such tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll discuss this in greater detail as well, so I don't want to dwell on it longer now. I would be interested in the following. Would you please explain to me what the ethnic structure was of the members of your police station.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: It was mixed. There were ethnic Albanians, Serbs, and Roma.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Can you give us the names of some of the members of your police station who were ethnic Albanians?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation] --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness start again. We did not hear the beginning.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Luri, Nazmi, Hysen, I cannot remember any more.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Not all names have been recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mladenovic, very briefly in relation to this topic, tell me, did Albanian pupils attend the state school in Stimlje; and if so, what is your source for this information?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In Stimlje, in addition to the police station of Stimlje, there was an elementary school. A large number of children attended that school from Stimlje itself and from the surrounding villages. The school worked all the way up until the beginning of the bombing on the 24th of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, members of the Albanian national minority, did they work in state institutions and state enterprises in the territory of Stimlje? Again, I'm asking you about your very own direct knowledge.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Albanians worked in state organs and organisations. Truth to tell, their numbers were somewhat smaller than in the 1990s. However, they had the same kind of jobs that the Serbs had. After what happened in 1998 and 1999, some of them received threats from Albanian terrorists. So in that period a number of them left their jobs in our state organs.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. How many policemen worked at your police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: 140. That was the total number including the active and reserve police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And how was work organised within your police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In the police station all this work that we mentioned a moment ago were carried out through patrols and through a sector-based type of work. That is how all our work was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned a few moments ago when you referred to the number of policemen in Stimlje, you mentioned active and reserve policemen. Did you have reserve policemen on your -- in your police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In the Stimlje police station we had members of the reserve police force as well. There were 70 of them, about 70, and 68 were active-duty policemen. That was their exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell me on the basis of whose orders members of the reserve force were engaged within your police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: All members of the reserve police force can be engaged only on orders from the minister. In my police station of Stimlje, they were engaged in that way too, the reservists, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But since we're talking about the number of reservists who are needed within the police station of Stimlje, how does one actually decide what that number will be, and do you play any role in that?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I think that this is regulated by some rules, but I believe that the ratio is one to one, that there can be one reserve police officer per active police officer so that it's roughly a one-to-one ratio.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Is there an interdependence, or rather, does the number of the -- did the strength of the reserve police depend on the security situation in the territory covered by police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Depending on the security situation and security-related problems, we filed an application for a certain number of reserve police officers to be called up. We forwarded that application to the department of the police and the SUP of Urosevac, and based on their assessments, I suppose that they asked the minister for approval; and having received it, they decided to call up a number of reserve police officers. It all went through the department of the police where there was an officer in charge of the reserve police. Everything we spoke about goes through the department of the police and the officer in charge of the reserve police force. As a police station we could only relay the security-related problems and ask for approval to use reserve police forces to carry out our security-related tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: When you speak about the security-related tasks, what kind of tasks exactly are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I'm always referring to our regular tasks and our regular work, which our -- for which we are responsible under the law. I can enumerate them.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now, that will not be necessary. Was there a special way of organising the personnel to go about their regular work and duties, given the fact that the reserve police were also used?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: The reserve police could not carry out any tasks independently. They did so with active police officers. The patrol leader was always an active police officer who only was assisted by a reserve police officer, and it was the active police officer who was responsible for their work. Reserve police officers were only used as assistants to the active police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know what reserve branch police stations were and what was their organisation?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Reserve branch police stations are a familiar notion. They existed in 1998 and 1999. We were unable to defend all the villages that were threatened by the Albanian terrorists, and therefore, some reserve police officers who hailed from those villages organised village guards for their homes and villages. They were armed. That was their role. And this went on until they were engaged as reserve forces of either the military or the police. Until that time they guarded their villages and homes. Among them, there were also armed Albanians and armed Serbs too. This part of the work also went via the department of the police and the officer in charge of these aspects, namely, the reserve personnel and reserve branch police stations. They had radio stations and were able to submit information regularly, report to us, so that we could come there fast to help them if necessary. At Muzicane, Rasince, Gornje Godance and Donje Godance, at Petrovic, and perhaps at other villages too, there were such organisations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. But let us be more precise for the sake of the transcript. My question and your answer do not refer to reserve police stations but reserve police departments?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. They did not have bases of their own, they didn't have facilities. They were locals who were simply at their homes and guarded their homes. They were self organised. They were self organised to protect their homes and villages, and the villages I listed, Muzicane, Rasince, Gornje Godance, Donje Godance, and Petrovic had such village guards, so in the day-time and in the night-time too police patrols would call on them and thus we provided protection to those villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the people who were members of reserve police departments, did they have their war time duties, and what would have happened if they -- or what would happen if they received calls to report?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they all had served in the army earlier and had their war time duties. So they belonged to either the police or the army as reserve forces. And if they should be called up under their war time duties, they were obliged to proceed in accordance with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain to me, you mentioned that the Albanian population was also armed when we were speaking about the reserve police departments. Can you clarify, and could you provide examples, who were these people?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: They were civilians who lived in those villages. They were loyal and hard-working citizens. They were afraid for their families. And since they were reserve police officers or reserve soldiers, they were armed as all other members of the reserve forces of either the police or the army. I now cannot remember everybody's names, but I remember the families Qeremi and Olluri, they were all of them practically involved. I didn't have the list nor did I keep a register. It was kept by the department of the police, the officer who was in charge there for the reserve forces and these reserve police departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please see document P257.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's number 2 in your binder, sir. Let me ask you some general questions. Did you have members of special police forces in your police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There were 11 uniformed police officers who were members of a special police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To which company did these police officers from the Stimlje police station belong?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not sure, but I believe that they were members of the 6th Company of the 24th Intervention Brigade, that's the Urosevac company. They were staff of that Urosevac company, and the company itself was part of the 124th Intervention Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Before we continue with the 124th Intervention Brigade, let me ask you whether you during your police career were ever a member of a special police unit?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was in 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: As members of this special police forces, did you ever take part in any special assignments in 1993 and 1994; if so, which?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of a special unit that would task -- that was tasked with breaking up the demonstrations in Belgrade. I believe that I was involved in such activities two times.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember when you were breaking up the demonstrations in Belgrade who commanded your unit which was brought there from Urosevac?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely because it was a long time ago, but I believe that there was a staff that commanded these special units. The staff was in Belgrade, but I don't remember who the commander was.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It isn't really necessary for you to remember the commander's name. It was quite some time ago. But these units, I mean the PJPs, were they used in all of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, they were established for the entire Republic of Serbia and they had the task of taking action in territories where the security situation demanded that. But this was directly controlled by the minister, so I don't to go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we'll see a document about that. Before that, tell me about these PJPs, were they regular police units, or were they established according to need?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: No. The PJPs are not regular police units. They are deployed depending on need.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As far as you know, in 1996, 1997, 1998, or 1999 were they used in the territory of the Republic of Serbia; and if so, what were the reasons for their use?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely where they were used, but in 1996 I think that they were used to provide security to certain personalities, on the occasion of demonstrations in Belgrade or Novi Sad, in Kosovo. And in 1998 and 1999 they were also used to combat terrorist activities, that is, in terrorism enforcement.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please now take a look at the exhibit that you have in front of you. This is a decision on the establishment of the 124th [Realtime transcript read in error "144th"] Intervention Brigade. Were the members of the PJPs from your police station part of the establishment of this brigade?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I think it doesn't say here, but they were members of the 6th Company of the 124th Brigade -- this brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I can see a mistake in the transcript. So the question was about the 124th intervention brigade of the PJP. Mr. Mladenovic, when they were not engaged as members of the PJPs, what were the tasks of those staff of your police station who were also members of the PJPs?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: When they were not engaged in their capacity of PJP members, they worked or they carried out their regular duties and tasks of their respective police stations. They had different tasks. Those from my police station were shift commanders, chiefs of sections, or regular police officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic. Tell me, we speak directly about the PJP members from the Stimlje police station. How did you call them up, based on whose orders, and where did you send them, referring to the PJP members from your police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I never received a written order for their engagement. That went through the SUP at Urosevac and the department of the police at Urosevac. Mostly it went like this: The chief of the department of the police, my immediate superior, informed me mostly over the phone. He would say when the members of the PJPs shall be prepared and inspected, and relocated to the respective PJP unit for subsequent tasks. Once we transferred them there, they carried out their respective assignments as commanded by their superiors. I mean the superiors from the PJP.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: What was the name of the commanding officer of that company of the PJP that included officers from your police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: The commander was Milan Lecic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you receive orders from the department of the police, yes, department of the police, what were you duty-bound -- what was your duty with regard to the preparation of the members of the PJP?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: My only duty was of a logistic nature. We should -- we were supposed to call them up, to inspect them with regard to their equipment and weapons, and transport them to the place they were supposed to report to carry out subsequent tasks. No more.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From the moment when members of the PJPs from your police station were sent in this way, what is their relationship towards you after that, in your capacity as commander of the Stimlje police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: From the moment when they are engaged in the special unit, when they report to the special unit, to the PJP, they had nothing more to do with me and our police station. From that moment onwards, I was no longer their superior officer, and I did not receive any reports about their further engagement or could I put any questions in that respect. Everything that had to do with discipline, criminal responsibility, et cetera, was transferred to the chief of SUP. I would receive information about that, though, because in accordance with the instructions on how to keep police station records, we kept a book of responsibility of our employees at the police station. That is why I could just receive information to the effect that, say, disciplinary proceedings were initiated against a member of the police station or for a minor infraction. Nothing that had to do with their specific tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: My direct question will be whether you received any information in relation to anti-terrorist actions or operations that were carried out by members of the PJPs from your police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: No. I did not receive such reports or were they duty-bound to report to me about their actions and operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, as you explained to us already, after you'd send these members of the PJPs would you submit any further reports to the police administration department?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: No. Since I received these orders orally, after sending the members of the PJPs from my police station further on, I only informed my superior over the telephone. At that time it was Radomir Mitic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Very briefly, what is it that you informed him about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In the briefest possible terms, that in accordance with his order members of the police were sent, as instructed, with equipment and arms to Urosevac. That is where they gathered most of the time and then they were engaged there. That would be it, that the task was accomplished as it had been set.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Bearing in mind what you just told us just now, who commanded the forces of the PJPs in the territory of Kosovo during 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: In the territory of Kosovo, the PJP forces were commanded by the staff for combatting terrorism of the MUP of the Republic of Serbia, headquartered in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Where do you get that knowledge, Mr. Mladenovic?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: From the collegium from the chief of SUP, Bogoljub Janicevic. We had regular collegium meetings there, and I regularly attended them on Mondays, sometimes even two or three times a week depending on the security situation and the problems that we had to resolve. At one of these meetings the chief informed us that the minister established a staff in Pristina to combat terrorism and that the commander of this staff was Major-General, as he was at the time, Sreten Lukic. And that that staff directly answered to the minister for all activities. They are subordinated to the minister, and the minister has direct control over the most important security problem that existed in that period of time in Kosovo. Also, all police units are subordinated to that staff, the staff for combatting terrorism in Kosovo and Metohija in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, did you tour your PJPs once they left, as you explained to us?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: No. I was not duty-bound to tour these units, and I did not do so. As a matter of fact, we were strictly prohibited from interfering in their work. That is to say that from the moment when they were engaged in a PJP, they -- we had no further obligation in relation to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you ever receive any tasks that were -- that would involve special security tasks? I'm referring to you and your police station and I'm not referring to the members of the PJPs.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: We never received such tasks. Our only task was to carry out those tasks that were prescribed by law. I referred to them a moment ago, and if necessary I'll go through it again. Our only duty was to do that. As a matter of fact, there was even an order to the effect that by no means should any persons who are not members of the PJPs be involved in tasks carried out by the PJPs and that we should not expose to further dangers our policemen who were not trained for carrying out such police work. That is to say that our only duty was to carry out the work specified in our rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D131, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's number 3 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: This document is under seal I am told, Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I assume that they are right. This is a document that was admitted into evidence when a protected witness was testifying. Therefore, I would suggest --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It should not be displayed outside the courtroom then.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would then kindly ask that we move into private session so that we can have a look at this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It should be able to be displayed within the courtroom, and I can see there are no people in a close position able to view the screens. So we will proceed on that basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, I'm now going to ask you to have a look at this Official Note dated the 28th of September, 1998. Could you please tell us briefly what this is all about. Could we hear your comments. Since this document is under seal, would you kindly not make any comments in relation to the actual names you will see in this document.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This document is an Official Note. It is a standard document that would be sent by a policeman who had carried out an official duty on the basis of the authority he had. It says here that a certain number of persons were brought in to custody at the police station in Stimlje, a certain number of persons were brought in. And these same persons were handed over to the crime police department of the Urosevac SUP. This had to be done whenever citizens would be brought in so that there would be records of that at the police station, that the persons were brought in and what happened to them afterwards. One copy accompanies the persons there -- mentioned therein, in this case SUP of Urosevac, for taking further action. These were probably persons who were linked to terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm now going to ask you to read to yourself, not aloud, please. Who compiled this Official Note and tell me yes or no as to whether you know this person, and we'll go into detail in closed session.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I know the person. This is a policeman from my police station. At that time, the police station in Stimlje.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at P1041.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's number 4 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, just a moment. I'm going to put some questions to you in this regard. The date is the 21st of October, 1998. The Ministry of the Interior, the staff of the ministry. What staff is referred to in the heading of this document, Mr. Mladenovic, do you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: That is the staff that was established in Pristina, the staff for combatting terrorism. I assume that that's that staff, the one from Pristina, because that's the only staff that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the first paragraph it is stated that in order to consistently implement tasks arising from the agreement on the OSCE mission in Kosovo and Metohija, it is necessary to undertake the following ..." Are you aware of the existence of this mission; and if so, can you tell us something about that in greater detail?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Of course I'm aware of the agreement. We called it the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement. That agreement allowed verifiers from the OSCE mission to verify everything that happened in Kosovo at the time. On the basis of this agreement verifiers were deployed throughout the territory of Kosovo. In the municipality of Stimlje I think that there were nine of them, including their commander, Tommy Olofsson [phoen] from Sweden. I was in contact with him most of the time. In accordance with this agreement, I could give you my further comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let's deal with it slowly. First of all, are you familiar with this dispatch, and did you see it at the time when it was sent?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I am familiar with it. All of us, all the secretariats, received it, all the police stations too because it had to do with what we were supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at (a) now, paragraphs 1, 2, and 3, it's on the first page. Please read it to yourself, and could we just hear your brief comment. What is it that this dispatch envisaged?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: As you can see, in this document members of the mission enjoyed diplomatic immunity, and they are allowed to move about and stay in the territory, and it is our duty to provide them all assistance in carrying out the tasks entrusted to them on the basis of the agreement. This also spells out in specific terms what the obligations of police stations are. At the request of members of the mission, they are duty-bound to give them all information that they seek. Also, they say what the level is because they were organised according to the same hierarchy as we were. They had their commander, deputy commander, et cetera. So contact was supposed to take place, as was the case in our country, commander with commander, deputy commander with the deputy commander, and so on. If the ranking officer is not there, then the next person in the chain was duty-bound to communicate with them and to give them all necessary information. On page 2 --

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us move on to page 2 of this document. So (b), reporting and information. What is this all about and what kind of reports did you send?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This is a continuation of the same document, and it has to do with the obligations of the organisation -- organisational unit, police station in my particular case. In terms of reporting and informing about provocations, attacks, movements, et cetera, we in the police station did not have such movements, so not everything pertained to us, but this was written for the entire secretariat. Then also there is a part that deals with resubordination, that they were being resubordinated as spelled out in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Number 2, police actions carried out.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This did not pertain to the Stimlje police station. I'm saying that this is a dispatch, a circulatory dispatch that was sent to all secretariats. So everyone reported from the point of view of their own province of work, the police station of Stimlje was not engaged in such actions and therefore did not report about any actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but let us be precise. When you say "to all secretariats," do you mean --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I mean all secretariats in Kosovo and Metohija, seven in all, Mitrovica, Pristina, Pec, Prizren, Urosevac, Gnjilane, and Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mladenovic, let me ask you whether you know that the road from Prizren through Suva Reka to Pristina was part of the agreement and providing security to that road was foreseen by the Clark-Naumann Agreement, as it was called. And this road was specially mentioned as a road to be controlled by the security forces of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I know that. I was informed about that at one of the regular meetings that we had with the chief of the secretariat of the SUP at Urosevac. I never saw the details of that agreement. But at the meeting we were told that under that agreement the highway was to be controlled by the police forces. That is, there was a temporary police squad to protect that road and some military forces were also to stay there to protect it. I believe that was made clear in the agreement, and the strength of those units was also determined.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: As you haven't seen that agreement, I will not show it to you now, but you knew that the units of the VJ were involved in the protection of that communication?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: And providing security to that road by the police, did it involve your police station in -- for part of that road, and how did you go about it?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: We had monitoring posts from Stimlje through Belince, Crnoljevo, along the road in the hills above the road, not on the road itself, and all the way to Dulje through the Crnoljevo canyon. Since this is a long stretch of road and the police station didn't have enough staff to carry out the task, it was decided at the level of the Urosevac SUP and probably at a higher level too, it -- that the SUP of Urosevac establish a company that will consist of active and reserve police officers and that was at the level of the entire SUP, which means that every police station, Stimlje, Strpce, Kacanik, and Urosevac shall provide one platoon each, one platoon of police which will make up a company. That company will deploy from Stimlje until Sumareva Kucica just outside Crnoljevo, whereas the Gnjilane company, which was also composed of reserve and active police officers, was deployed from Sumarevo Kucica all the way to Dulje, but not on the road itself but in the hills above it. Mostly we took possessions of the trenches that had been dug by the Albanian terrorists in -- when they wanted to block that road. Our units were at observation posts to provide security to that road. That was the only task of these temporary police squads, and certainly there was traffic police that controlled the entire highway.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, but when you were speaking about providing security and observation posts that were there, were you referring to regular police duties that were part of the public security sector?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. These were regular duties, and they were carried out by regular units. They were not members of PJPs nor were they involved in any combat operations. Their only task was to be deployed at the locations laid out in the agreement and the monitors verified that together with us and they were present until just before the bombing.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Exhibit D136 was also admitted under seal. It's a document dated the 6th of November, 1998. I believe the situation is the same as with the previous document. It contains some brief information, or rather, I would like to ask some brief questions to elicit information about its contents. But as it's almost time for the break, I don't know whether We should do that now or later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will have the break. We will resume at a quarter past 4.00. At that time the document can be displayed in the court and not outside of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Could we please have D132. It was under seal, hence I would kindly ask that it only be broadcast within the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, that is your tab 6. It is dated the 6th of November, 1998. We see that the title is Official Note on intelligence in connection with organising of terrorists in the village of Racak. Could you please read out the document for yourself and comment on it. Can you tell us whether you had information of this nature about Racak.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: "On 6 November 1998, through a friendly source I obtained information that on the right side along the stretch of the road leading from the village of Petrovo to the village of Racak, Stimlje SO, Siptar terrorists were digging trenches and constructing bunkers and that they were felling lots of trees for the construction of the bunkers." This is an operational document submitted by a member of the police station in Stimlje. This was an illustration of the events from that time. In that period, November 1998, Albanian terrorists in the villages erected fortifications and bunkers which they used to attack and offer resistance to the state authorities. They attacked civilians and all those trying to use the nearby roads. This is not the only operational document which we received. It is one out of many that were drafted by the policemen at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. To support that I would kindly ask to have D133 displayed. According to the information I have, this document was not under seal. It is your tab 7. It is dated 18 November 1998. Please look at the first paragraph. You don't have to read it out loud, only to yourself, and please offer your comment. In particular, can you tell us whether this tallies with the information you had about Racak at that time.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This document was drafted by the SUP in Urosevac and sent to the MUP staff for the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija and Pristina. Its contents speak of the villages around Racak as well as the villages around Stimlje, out of which civilians were moving out for reasons of fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Please focus on the second sentence in the first paragraph, which says: "... KLA had come to Racak village and ordered the locals to leave the village because greater numbers of them wanted to move into it."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: That is correct. They ordered the same thing in each and every village where they planned to set up their strongholds. Civilians, of course, fled such areas, foreseeing clashes between the KLA and the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we next please have 65 ter document 1187 from the Defence list, which is D008-5625. That is the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Mladenovic, it is your tab 8. We see that this is a statement on the 22nd of November, 1998. This is the date of the statement. Please look at the second paragraph. Read it and comment on it briefly. But before that, just have a look at who the authorised officials are at the bottom of the document, Jasovic and Sparavalo.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This statement was taken from -- should I mention the name or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: You may do so.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Mustafa Metush. He is from Racak, the municipality of Stimlje. The statement was taken in the crime police department. The two people mentioned, Mr. Jasovic and Sparavalo were two crime inspectors in the Urosevac SUP. As for Mustafa Metush, he stated that Isak Musliu, a.k.a. Qerqiz, held a meeting in the mosque. He requested that the locals provide funds, 200 German marks each, which were to be used to buy weapons. They used the same system in many villages. They would gather assets and use such monies to buy weapons. Each inhabitant of the villages had to also participate in the digging of trenches and erecting bunkers for their needs. Whoever lacked funds had to provide them with oil, flour, or foodstuffs. There were also individuals who had machinery, such as tractors and diggers, which they had to use to dig trenches and roads for the use of the KLA. There is a path or a road between Rance and Jezerce which was made by KLA members with the assistance of locals. There was much discussion about this because people were already going through lots of hardship, and yet they had to dedicate certain funds for their needs. Whoever disobeyed, things happened to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Please look at the penultimate paragraph. Read it to yourself again and comment, please. Did you have such information at the time?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This is correct, I suppose, because many houses at that time had been abandoned by the locals who were fearful of clashes between the terrorists and police. Such empty houses, which were not under the protection of the police station because they couldn't be due to their location, became criminal targets. Such houses were looted by people from that or nearby villages. That is why the abandoned house is mentioned here, and it is stated that such houses are being looted. It doesn't say by whom, but it was probably by such groups. This is what was taking place at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we see a certain Mehmet Cazimi and Idriz Mehmeti mentioned in the same paragraph. It says they lived on the hill above the old folks' home, and I know that they have committed many crimes stealing from the abandoned houses in Racak?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Is that correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I seek to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, it will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00818.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have D135 displayed.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 10, Mr. Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just been notified that it's not under seal. I think we agree that it is not under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is hardly legible. It is your tab 10, and the document is dated 18 December 1998. It says here: "Several short bursts of fire were opened from Racak village on the Stimlje police station. Members of the police did not respond to the fire." Signed by sergeant first class Svetomir Bocic. Can you please comment on what is contained in the document.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This is probably a dispatch sent from the duty office of the Urosevac SUP to the staff. In signature we have Svetomir Bocic. I know him in person. He was the shift leader in the Urosevac SUP. This event was recorded in our police station, I recall it. The attack came from the village of Racak. At the time in Racak there were certain terrorist groups stationed there. We had a forward security detail of a SUP building which was attacked from their positions. The attack was registered, but we did not return fire. I think this was also discussed later with the verifiers. This dispatch was sent to the staff as a regular dispatch on daily events in connection with the previous information on the types of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think we can see that in this document, hence it is your presumption?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. We also cannot see any stamps here.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we next have D136. It is your tab 11. Have a look at page 2 of the document, please, and confirm to us whether you indeed drafted and signed this document.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the signature is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is a report on contact with members of the OSCE mission dated 21 December 1998. First of all, please explain to us how you communicated with OSCE mission members.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: We communicated with them as of the moment of their arrival. This is of course concerning my area, the area of the municipality and police station of Stimlje. We agreed on the times that we were to meet. At first it was daily, but later on, due to the increasing work burden on our part it was on Mondays and Fridays. And of course as the situation required in case there were more serious incidents and cases of disturbing law and order.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us comment on a few things. First of all, tell us who did you send this report to?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: My obligation as an authorised official was to report on every contact we had with the OSCE to the chief of the police department. There was a conversation I had with the OSCE members, which is what I wrote this report on and forwarded it to the SUP in Urosevac, and I believe they would then forward such information to the staff although it's my assumption only.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It seems everything is in the transcript. In the first paragraph it says "without prior notice."

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was according to the agreement. They did not need to notify us in advance when they wanted to establish contact or when they wanted to inquire about a certain event. They were free to visit at any time of day or night. They could enter the police station and request that they see someone to whom they could put questions. It says here that this was without prior notice and on their initiative. We can see from the document what they wanted to discuss.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: I'll lead you through it. I'm interested in the mid-paragraph on the first page. The sentence begins with "also." You don't need to read it out loud. Please provide a comment only because you mention here that members of all ethnic communities in the territory of Stimlje were under threat by the terrorists in the villages of Racak, Petrovo, and Crnoljevo?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the three villages are referred to because from those villages there were constant provocations and attacks on the members of the police. We shared this piece of information with them, hoping that they would forward it appropriately to their own superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The last sentence in the -- that paragraph, read it to yourself, you mention two attacks of the 17th and the 20th of December, one from the village of Racak, the other from Crnoljevo. Can you please comment briefly. Is this what the situation was like in the territory of the Stimlje police station?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The situation was such, and I state here that they attacked in depth, which is something that is connected with the previous dispatch. We informed the staff about this. The other attack was on a check-point where a police patrol was located in charge of securing the town. So these two armed attacks were registered, and the information was shared with the verifiers. We did not respond to these attacks, and we did not undertake any further action. On page 2 it says that there was an explosion about 50 metres from the check-point. This was probably a shell that exploded which had been launched from a hand-held launcher or a weapon of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you say 50 metres from the check-point?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, 50 metres, not kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please go to D007-0120.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It is your tab 12. Mr. Mladenovic, this is a criminal report dated 3 January 1999. It is stated that on the 2nd of January, 1999, in Stimlje on Lipljanski Put in front of a family house, Enver Gashi was killed by terrorists, by automatic weapons. What operational data did you have about this event, and do you recall it at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I remember the event. This happened on New Year's day, that is, on the 2nd of January, 1999, but it was a public holiday. Operative information indicated that Albanian terrorists shot Enver Gashi with the intention of killing him because he was loyal to the authorities. The -- this man Enver Gashi was a car mechanic and used to repair cars in front of his house, even our official vehicles. He was a fair man, and we supposed that this was the reason why they killed him. Whoever co-operated with the police and was an Albanian suffered their -- from their vengeance. We can see that this document was signed by the authorised official DS. It stands for Dostan Sabani. This must have been forwarded to the district prosecutor in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you just repeat the name of the police inspector who filed this report.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Dostan Sabani.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now it's all right.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: He was inspector for violent crime and sexual offences.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender this document into evidence, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit D00819.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Now let's take a look at Exhibit D137. Mr. Mladenovic, you can find it under tab 13. You can go to the second page of the document immediately and tell us whether this is your signature and whether you drafted this document.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's my signature, and I drafted this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I want to go back to the first page. It's dated the 4th of January, 1995. It's a report on the meeting with members of the OSCE version mission. Let me focus your attention on the second paragraph. It starts by: "At the moment when the OSCE verifiers arrived and asked for a meeting in my office there was Ibish Qari," if I'm not mistaken, and it goes on to say more about that meeting. Can you tell us if you remember what this is about?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This is a document which like the reports on all these meetings was forwarded to the secretariat at Urosevac. It's about the arrival of the OSCE verifiers without prior notice, and when they arrived Mr. Ibish Qari born in 1937 was in my office. He was an old man. He was going to Racak or Petrovo to visit his daughter who was married there. And on the road to Petrovo in the village of Malo Poljce he was kidnapped by the members of the terrorist KLA. There was even information to the effect that Sadik Mujota and his sons were the perpetrators. They kidnapped him and kept him in a barn of some kind, he was - he isn't sure. They blindfolded him, and he kept him there for ten days and he only received food and water once a day. He somehow managed to escape and then came to the police station to report the event. And I was speaking to him in my office when the verifiers of the OSCE mission arrived, and thus I gave them an opportunity to get first-hand information about these events. I don't know what else I could add.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: In the last paragraph you say that you informed the OSCE mission members of several terrorist attacks?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Here it says that the inspectors of the OKP of Urosevac of the -- Musa and Vitomir Naskovic were also present during the conversation and so were the verifiers of the OSCE mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic. Now please look at the following page of the document.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: What's your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let us wait for the document to appear on the screen. My question is: You say that Ibish Qari reported his kidnapping at the Stimlje police station and asked the MUP's assistance to protect him from the terrorist gangs who had kidnapped him and who had threatened him, threatened him that they would kill him if he were to report the kidnapping to the police. Please comment what this says.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's exactly how it was. His report was not only a formal act. He came and -- to ask for protection because they had threatened him. If he were to report the fact that he was kidnapped and detained, that they would kill his family. He wanted to see his daughter who was married at -- in one of these villages. He requested protection from the police. His house was in Stimlje, so we visited him regularly. So he was safe in his house, but his movement if he was going to Racak or elsewhere was very risky. Not only for him but for all loyal citizens. So we gave him advice not to go there, and we provided protection to his family throughout the time we were there, that is, until the 12th of June, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see Exhibit D139.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This is under tab 14 in your binder. Mr. Mladenovic, this is a report on sighting or contact with members of the OSCE mission dated 10 January 1999. A terrorist attack on the members of the police station of Stimlje is mentioned, and it goes on to say that the OSCE verifiers learned the name of the injured police officer who was transferred to Pristina hospital. Do you remember this event?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I remember the event. I just want to comment on this report. It is signed by Sasa Draskovic. At the time he was assistant commander of the Urosevac police station and Svetislav Przic was then a police officer of the Stimlje police station. He was lethally wounded on the 10th of January, 1999, in the village of Slivovo while he was going home. There were also Nenad Mitrovic, the deputy commander, and Miroslav Zivic. They -- all three of them were in a vehicle travelling from Stimlje to Urosevac, that is, going home. In Slivovo which is after Kosare, between Kosare and Urosevac, they were ambushed, the vehicle was hit and Przic suffered lethal injuries. Just a moment if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: We can go into more detail because the following document speaks in more detail about this very event, so in order to save time, can we now see Exhibit D138, which is under tab 15 in your binder. If we could look at -- yes, this is the document. Let's go to page 2 immediately. This is a criminal report, and you can go on with your comment because this is related to what you were saying.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: This is a criminal report filed by -- filed to the secretariat in Urosevac. After an on-site investigation at the site of the crime. This report proves that the OSCE verifiers immediately upon learning that a police patrol had been attacked wanted to go there in person to get first-hand information. And this is a criminal report which after the on-site investigation had been completed -- this criminal report was drafted.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: If we look at the second page of the same document we see that there are -- there's a protocol of the on-site investigation.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: This also says that the site of the attack was the Muslim cemetery which is in the immediate vicinity of the road. Could you explain exactly where that was? We saw documents about Racak and now this is the section of the road towards Urosevac.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: The inspectors of the OKP of Urosevac speak about the direction from Urosevac to Stimlje, the village of Slivovo, which is on this main road. And this Muslim cemetery, so a religious facility, is on the left side if you look from Urosevac toward Stimlje. It is in the immediate vicinity of the road and there is a groove there. I used to pass by there all the time because my house is near that village in Urosevac town. I passed there regularly, so -- well, I don't think I should comment any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us now take a look at Exhibit D140.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It's under tab 16 in your binder. The document has only one page, it's one page long. It's your report. You can check the signature. Is it your signature?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, this is my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: It was drafted upon the contact you had with the OSCE verification mission, and it's dated 11 January 1999. Please read the first paragraph to yourself and comment on it, especially with regard to the claims of the verifiers who say that it was peaceful earlier in the area of Stimlje, whereas the situation at that moment was tense. So please comment on these allegations.

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that was their comment, that allegedly the situation in Racak was calm, whereas now it was -- it was tense. I explained to them that the situation was by no means calm. How could it be if our surrounding villages there were terrorist fortifications and all the population of those villages had moved out? The women and children had left the houses in 1998, so most of the houses in Petrovo, Malo Poljce, Racak, Rance, Zborce, Duga, Karacica, Petrastica and Crnoljevo were empty. These were villages near the hills, and there were strong terrorists -- strongholds there. So in this text I stated that their allegations were not correct, that many people had been kidnapped, and that Albanian terrorists attack innocent civilians, the army, and the police from those villages. So this is one of these documents, and I forwarded this report to the department of the police, that is, to my base as stated in the instruction I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Speaking about these women and children who left their houses in 1998 from Petrovo, Malo Poljce, Racak, Rance, and so on, where did those people go?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: The people from those villages didn't go far then. They descended to Stimlje because the town of Stimlje was secured much better so that all those civilians were either in Stimlje or with relatives in Urosevac, Lipljan, Pristina, or Suva Reka, Prizren, depending on where they have relatives. But mostly they were there. Sometimes they would go to their village to see their house, but then they would be kidnapped or mistreated or detained there. So most families took their women and children to towns or villages which were better protected by the police. For the most part, they were put up in Stimlje, but some went to Urosevac or Lipljan or Suva Reka. So that would be my answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mladenovic. Now we have come to the events in the village of Racak. Tell me, do you know anything about the events that occurred in Racak on the 15th of January, 1999, or rather, chronologically speaking what happened, where you were at the time, what you did, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of January, 1999, at 6.00 in the morning I was at the Urosevac SUP where I was supposed to take over a company of a temporary police squad in Crnoljevo and to replace my men who had already been in Crnoljevo. The company gathered at the Urosevac SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, are we talking here about a temporary police squad?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In that squad we took turns every 15 days, Stimlje, Strpce, Kacanik, and Urosevac, commanders were company commanders. We changed every 15 days and the personnel changed every 15 days too. So it was our duty to take the company at the SUP of Urosevac, and then we'd go on that shift together with our men; and 15 days later we would go back with our men. On that day I was supposed to leave at 6.00 a.m. in order to be at that position by 7.00 and that we carry out the hand-over of duty. At that time we could not leave because I was informed by an officer from the police station that a blockade had been carried out by the traffic police of the Urosevac SUP on the main road between Urosevac and Stimlje and Crnoljevo near the village of Kosare. And therefore, the company could not go out while that was still the case. I had no idea at the time what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Let us just be very specific with regard to some matters and then we'll go on. Tell me, when you say that you received information from the officer at the police station as recorded here --

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: -- tell us, what officer, if you remember. Not the name and surname, but rather, what was that officer who provided you with that information, what was his duty?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: It was Milivoj Nedeljkovic. I remember he was an officer of the branch police station. He was in charge of legality of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any information about that, what kind of action is underway, what is going on, and why the blockade had been placed there?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: I did not have any contacts or did anyone inform me about that. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. POPOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, please go ahead. What happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: BRANKO MLADENOVIC
utterances.text: The entire company stayed there until the same officer let us know that we could go and start our shift. That's when we set out, that's when I led the company. I think it was around 8.30 in the morning. When I arrived to that point there were quite a few vehicles that were still waiting. They were waiting to be allowed to proceed, civilian vehicles, that is. I think that we spent some time there then and that then the order arrived to the effect that traffic would be allowed on the road in both directions. I then went with my column to Stimlje, and I stopped there for about half an hour because I was supposed to take over part of the equipment for Stimlje for the platoon that was in Stimlje. It had to do with some personal affairs that we needed to take out into the field for cooking, et cetera. When I entered the police station in Stimlje, in my office I found the chief of SUP, Bogoljub Janicevic and Radomir Mitic, the head of the police department.
